zones.label: Column 1, part 1
zones.note: Lexical aid consulted after scan reading: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0. Supplied page subset; https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . The scan remains the authority for text and typography.

lines.note: This continuation describes a shrine or hermitage of the kami. Camis belongs to the Portuguese explanation of the preceding page's entry; it is not a new headword.
Igaua denotes a well. Meliùs recommends Inomoto as the preferable word; the grave accent and historical Portuguese Poço are retained.

runs.text: E o de mais. l, &c. palaura que ſe

lines.note: Igue is explained as the remainder or "and so forth." The scan separates E o and prints de mais; this is not the OCR's single word Eo.

runs.text: vſa no cabo de outras como, &c. ¶

lines.note: The explanatory phrase says that Igue is used at the end of other expressions, like "etc." The paragraph sign introduces the separate example Igue-no mono across the physical break.
No mono completes the preceding example, referring to people of lower standing. The Portuguese supplies both "lesser" and "inferior," rather than simply another "etc." example.
This homonymous Igue means a thorn. The regional comparison says that Cami uses Igui; both Japanese forms must remain distinct from the previous Igue entry.

Iguen concerns displaying power and pomp with arrogance. The Portuguese construction continues on the next line; fausto retains the provisional st classification rather than being globally regularized.
Arrogancia completes the definition. The two illustrated constructions use iguen with suru and, across the next break, with yuu; the alternative marker l is not a Japanese letter.
Uo yǔ completes the second construction, "speak arrogantly." The caron over u is visible and is not a Portuguese accent or an abbreviation tilde.
Igueuara is a thorn thicket or place full of thorns, extending the preceding thorn vocabulary. The initial is a capital I in the scan, not the OCR's lowercase i.
Igui is paraphrased by Cotonaru gui and concerns irrelevant or inappropriate matters. Gui is the Japanese noun in the paraphrase, not a Portuguese word or a mistaken qi.
The Portuguese adds "things that do not fit." Iguiuo iuaſuna begins the prohibition against speaking such matters, with the long s belonging to the Japanese verb form.

runs.text: Não o deixes falar de cà, &

lines.note: Xibare and tataqe are imperatives, "bind" and "strike." The Portuguese begins an expanded rendering of the preceding prohibition and continues its explanation below.

runs.text: de là. i, couſas fora de propoſito, prende,

lines.note: The Portuguese identifies the speech as irrelevant talk and then says "arrest/bind." This is a continuation of the same Japanese example, not an independent definition.
Dalhe completes the command to strike the person. Although short, the row is genuine body text and must not be merged into the following saddle entry.
Igui, alternatively yugui, denotes a wooden part of the saddle seat. The printed aßento retains its ligature representation rather than being expanded or modernized.
This separate Igui is a fish name. The scan shows initial I, not lowercase l; the gloss gives no diagnostic description that would justify assigning a modern species.
Another Igui means a thorn, with Igue identified as the Ximo equivalent. This reverses the regional comparison in c1-l006 and confirms that the similar entries are not duplicates.
Iguinǒ is glossed "without danger." The unusual romanized form and its caron are retained; the generated reading is an aid, not authority to normalize the headword.

Iguiǒ and Cotonaru catachi concern a different shape. The worn initial I is recoverable. At the expected r in Diuerſa there are faint compatible ink remnants; this damaged-letter reconstruction is preferred to treating the gap as a deliberately omitted letter, but remains uncertain.
The example pairs Iguiǒ with iru-i and is translated as different forms and species. The hyphen inside iru-i is printed internally; no terminal hyphen is supplied after eſpe.
Cies completes eſpe-cies from the preceding row, followed by "of animals." The physical division is retained even though the word was not visibly hyphenated at the right edge.
This homonymous Iguiǒ is paraphrased Yaſui voconai: easy practices or deeds. It is semantically distinct from the preceding different-shape entry despite identical spelling.
Faceis completes "exercises or deeds that are easy." Its position as a short continuation, rather than a new entry, is preserved.
Iguiri denotes boring with a gimlet, and X. identifies the regional usage. The following Cami comparison continues below; the roman X. is kept outside the italic Portuguese span.
The Cami alternatives are Qirimomu and Anauo aquru, both describing boring or opening a hole. They complete the Portuguese phrase "is called" on this row.

runs.text: Ponta de huns paos a traueſados na

lines.note: Igui ſaqi denotes the projecting ends of saddle timbers. The scan retains a space in a traueſados; it is not silently regularized to the modern single-word spelling.
The relative clause says that those transverse saddle timbers project outward. The doubled l in ſella is retained, although the earlier saddle gloss uses ſela.
Iguiſu denotes a kind of marine weed. The Japanese long s and the Portuguese historical plural limos are preserved without imposing a modern botanical identification.
Igo is equated with Nochi, "after" or "onward." This temporal entry is separate from the following identical-looking headword with another meaning.
The second Igo is glossed "another statement/opinion." The short independent entry must not be absorbed into the temporal sense above.
Iguai and Cocorono foca express something beyond what one expected. The printed doque is joined, and the Portuguese first-person sense is supplied by cuidaua.
Igi concerns disposition or temperament. The example contrasts a person of good or bad disposition; the scan shows one tilde over the o in Condiçaõ, not the OCR's double-marked ending.

runs.text: Homem de boa condiçaõ, ou ruim.

lines.note: The Portuguese completes the contrast between a good-natured person and a bad-tempered one. The printed condiçaõ again places the tilde on the final vowel.

IIen means "before." A two-line enlarged I belongs before the smaller Ien, yielding IIen rather than the OCR's Ien; the supplied NINJAL index independently corroborates the lexical form after scan reading.
Iji is glossed "physician." The line is offset to make room for IIen's enlarged initial; the initial does not belong to this second headword or create another letter here.

runs.text: Em ſũma. l, reſumindo, ou aſomãdo.

lines.note: Ijǒ is glossed "in sum," "summing up," or "adding together." The headword's j descender and capital I correct the OCR's iiǒ; the nasal abbreviations in ſũma and aſomãdo remain unexpanded.
This Ijǒ concerns differing from someone's wishes, paraphrased Tagǒ cocoro. The caron on Tagǒ is visible; the Portuguese clause continues into the next row.
The continuation specifies someone's heart or intention. Coraçaõ carries a single tilde on o, rather than the OCR's two accented vowels.

runs.text: Fortaleza onde reſide o capitaõ como em

lines.note: This further Ijǒ denotes the stronghold where a captain resides. Its meaning is not the preceding disagreement sense, and the Portuguese dwelling comparison continues below.
Proprias caſas completes the explanation: the stronghold serves as the captain's own home. This short continuation belongs wholly to the preceding Ijǒ entry.
Ijǔ is paraphrased Cotonaru qedamono and glossed "other animals." The scan supports Ijǔ rather than riǔ; the accent belongs to u, and qedamono must not be changed to a g spelling.
The fifth letter of ANTFS has an F-like outline with no secure lower arm. The aligned draft's F is retained rather than silently normalizing the heading to ANTES; a worn E remains possible.
IMa means "now" and, in compounds, "more" or "another." The enlarged two-line I omitted by OCR is restored before Ma, with the capital M retained.

The row completes ſigni-fica and starts the example Imà fitotçuno, "one more." The a is heavily damaged; the draft's grave is retained because a small compatible mark survives, though its identity is uncertain. The word is roman, and the row is indented beside the enlarged initial.

Mais hum translates the example at the foot of column 1. The next example asks someone honorifically to drink once more; qicoxime- continues with xe below, and the visible terminal hyphen replaces OCR punctuation.

Xe completes qicoximexe, the honorific imperative. The Portuguese says "drink once more." The fresh scan pass does not establish a separate wordspace between mais and hũa, so the draft's tight maishũa join is retained rather than imposing a modern boundary; the nasal abbreviation is not expanded.

runs.text: Certa laya de cortinas que ſe armão ao

lines.note: Imacu denotes a kind of curtain or screen. The explanation begins to describe how the curtains are erected around a vessel or encampment.

runs.text: derre dor nas bordas da embarcação, ou no

lines.note: The curtains are set around the edges of a vessel. The visibly separated derre dor is preserved as printed, rather than silently joined to derredor.
Arrayal completes the alternative location, an encampment. Its historical y spelling and the concluding etcetera remain part of the preceding definition.

runs.text: Adu. Ainda não: ſempre ſe junta com

lines.note: Imada means "not yet." The dictionary labels it an adverb and begins a grammatical note about its use with negative forms.

runs.text: negatiuo na terminação da eſcritura. Vt,

lines.note: The note specifies a negative ending in written usage. The worn Portuguese word is eſcritura, not OCR eſcritara; the italic Vt introduces the Japanese example.
Tenca imada xizzumarazu says that the realm is not yet pacified. The Portuguese translation repeats Tenca, abbreviating its nasal with a tilde and dividing it as Tẽ-ca across the row boundary.
Ca completes the embedded name Tenca. The remainder describes the realm as not yet quiet and peaceful; this is still the translation of the preceding Japanese sentence.
Ima faya means "already now" or "now at last." The example begins ima haya ando itaita, whose verb is completed on the following row.
Itaita completes the historical past form in the example, giving the sense "now I am at ease." It is not corrected to a modern Japanese verb ending.

runs.text: Adu. Por agora, ou neste tẽpo.

lines.note: Ima fodo refers to the present time or "for now." The abbreviation Adu. is grammatical apparatus; the Portuguese nasal abbreviation in tẽpo is retained.
Imagoro is another adverb with the preceding time-reference sense. Idem explicitly refers back to Ima fodo rather than starting a new explanation.
Imaichiuǒ means "once more." The capital I and Portuguese Outra are recoverable from the scan; the repeated Japanese example corroborates the worn headword without dictating its typography.
Mǒſǒzu completes "I shall say/tell it once more." Both o marks are carons in the scan; the first is not the circumflex supplied by OCR.
Imaimaxij describes something ominous or ill-omened. The apparent extra initial I in OCR is part of the nearby column rule; the Japanese example starts Sayǒ- and continues below.
The example says not to speak such ominous things. Its visibly spaced ima imaxij is retained, as is the honorific negative command vôxeraruruna, rather than being modernized.

runs.text: Não faleis eſſas couſas de ruim agouro.

lines.note: The Portuguese translates the warning not to utter things of bad omen. The paired long s letters in eſſas are retained independently of the Japanese spelling above.
Imaimaxiſa and Imaimaxǔ give the nominal and adverbial derivatives of the adjective. There is no paragraph sign before them in this impression, so the OCR's added sign is removed.

runs.text: Embarcação de hũa ſoo taboa por bãda.

lines.note: Imaixen is a vessel with only one plank on each side. The scan prints ſoo with two o letters, rather than OCR ſo; taboa and bãda retain their historical forms.
Imani covers "now" and "up to now." The example that follows specifies the latter sense rather than treating these Portuguese glosses as interchangeable in every context.
Imani itaru made means "up to the present." The Portuguese Tegora and tè eſte tẽpo express the same endpoint, with their spelling and abbreviated nasal retained.
Imaſara means "now, at this stage." The example begins a statement about there no longer being a way to explain something; the capital I and long s are visible.
The Japanese says there is no way to explain or state it now. The Portuguese begins "now one cannot"; po continues as de on the next row, with no terminal hyphen supplied without ink evidence.
De completes pode from the preceding line. Dar razão and declarar explain the same Japanese expression as giving an account or making the matter clear.
Imauaxij is cross-referenced to Imaimaxij as having the same ominous sense. The second Japanese form is embedded in the explanatory Idem, quod construction, not a second headword.

runs.text: Caixas fundidas de nouo, ou dagora.

lines.note: Imaxen refers to newly cast cash, with fundidas and the sen element pointing to coinage rather than ordinary boxes. The printed Portuguese word remains Caixas; this contextual interpretation does not alter it.
Imaxime with its principal forms is defined as "prohibit." The inflectional abbreviations uru and eta belong to the Japanese verb, not to the Portuguese gloss.
The nominal Imaxime is "prohibition." Its independent entry separates the noun from the adjacent verb entries.
A second verbal Imaxime means "bind or tie up." Yocu- starts the reduplicated adverb in the example, which continues on the next physical row.
Yocuyocu imaximete voqe instructs that the person or object be tied securely. The Portuguese Ponde o amarrado is preserved with its printed spacing rather than silently recast as modern Portuguese.
Bem, & arecado completes the instruction to bind securely and keep safe. The joined historical arecado is retained rather than expanded into a modern phrase.
Imaxiua is a poetic expression for "now." The upright P. is a usage label, distinct from the italic Portuguese Agora.
Imayǒ concerns something currently in fashion or circulation. Its example specializes the sense to a contemporary song or tune, rather than every possible kind of novelty.

runs.text: Cantar com toada noua que ago-

lines.note: Uo vtǒ completes the instruction or description of singing an imayō. The Portuguese explains singing a new, current tune; ago- is visibly divided before ra below.
Ra completes agora and closes the current-tune explanation. This short row remains a continuation of the Imayǒ example.
Imayori means "from now onward." The scan's joined pordiante is retained as historical spelling, and Adu. remains italic grammatical apparatus.
Imayori igo is given the same "from now onward" sense. Both Japanese components belong to the phrase, while Idem refers to the preceding gloss.
Imayori nochi is another expression for "henceforth." Nochi reinforces the temporal sense rather than introducing an unrelated noun entry here.
Imayori xiteua receives the same gloss. The printed phrase is retained without inserting a modern morphological boundary into xiteua.
Imeǒ is paraphrased Cotonaru na, a different or additional name. The Portuguese begins an explanation of names bestowed because of a characteristic or occasion.

runs.text: algũa manha, ſinal, ou outra occaſião, &c.

lines.note: The names may refer to a habit, identifying mark, or other circumstance. Algũa keeps the tilde over u, and the explanation does not warrant reducing the term simply to a personal name.
Imi gives the verb imu, associated with taboo or avoidance. The example begins a medicine's incompatibility with metal or fire, with ca- continuing as neuo below.

Neuo completes caneuo, the object referring to metal; fiuo imu is the alternative concerning fire. The Portuguese begins to describe an incompatibility of the medicine rather than prescribing a treatment.

runs.text: contrariedade com o ferro, ou com o fogo. i,

lines.note: The Portuguese specifies an incompatibility with iron or fire. The following i, introduces a further explanation of the recorded belief.

runs.text: Se ſe corta com ferro, ou poem ao fogo perde a

lines.note: The explanation says that cutting with iron or putting it on the fire causes loss of efficacy. The apparent final l in OCR is the column rule, not text; the line ends with the article a.

runs.text: virtude, ou faz mal a quem atoma.

lines.note: Virtude completes the loss-of-efficacy statement, with an alternative that the medicine harms its taker. The joined atoma is preserved; the isolated Imi below is a catchword, not an additional body entry.
